name: Anita Carleton
milestone_by_age_26: No birth year documented in reviewed sources; major recognitions (IEEE Fellow 2022, SEI Fellow 2024) and her 1999 book on software process measurement arrived in mid/late career. Cannot verify any material milestone by age 26.
early_history_summary: Anita D. Carleton studied applied mathematics at Carnegie Mellon and earned an MBA from MIT Sloan. She worked on missile systems software at GTE and tire modeling at Goodyear before joining the Software Engineering Institute in the late 1980s, later directing the Software Solutions Division and co-authoring Measuring the Software Process (1999).
evidence_summary: Wikipedia and SEI materials document her SEI leadership and late-career fellowships but omit birth year and any dated early-career breakthrough. Without age anchors, eligibility cannot be established.

name: Peter Zijlstra
milestone_by_age_26: No birth year found in reviewed sources; first real kernel patches came ~10 years after mid-1990s Linux introduction (~2005–2006 era). Without a confirmed birth year, a material milestone by age 26 cannot be established.
early_history_summary: Peter Zijlstra is a professional Linux kernel hacker at Intel OTC, known as a core maintainer of the Linux scheduler and contributor to VM and real-time subsystems. He has spoken widely at Linux Plumbers and related conferences.
evidence_summary: LWN and conference bios describe his kernel path but provide no birth year. Material visibility as scheduler maintainer is a multi-year technical career achievement without a dated ≤26 milestone.

name: Sarita Adve
milestone_by_age_26: No birth year documented; B.Tech IIT Bombay 1987, PhD Wisconsin–Madison 1993, Rice faculty from 1993, NSF CAREER 1995. Major awards (Maurice Wilkes 2008, Ken Kennedy 2018) came well after typical age 26; without birth year eligibility cannot be verified.
early_history_summary: Sarita Vikram Adve earned a B.Tech in electrical engineering at IIT Bombay (1987) and MS/PhD in CS at Wisconsin–Madison (1989/1993). She was faculty at Rice (1993–1999) before joining UIUC, where she is the Richard T. Cheng Professor working on architecture, parallel computing, and memory models.
evidence_summary: Wikipedia and ACM award pages give a clear academic timeline but no birth year. PhD and first faculty job in 1993 would need birth ≤1967 to fall at ≤26; that is not established. Fame and major awards are mid-career.

name: Martin Fowler
milestone_by_age_26: Born 1963; graduated UCL 1986 (age ~22) and worked at Coopers & Lybrand, then independent consulting from 1991 (age ~27). First major book Analysis Patterns (1996, age ~32); Refactoring (1999, age 35); Agile Manifesto co-author 2001 (age 37). No material field-defining milestone by age 26 found.
early_history_summary: Martin Fowler grew up in Walsall, England, attended Queen Mary's Grammar School, and earned a BSc in Electronic Engineering and Computer Science from UCL (1983–86). After Coopers & Lybrand and a small tech firm, he became an independent consultant in 1991, moved to Massachusetts in 1994, and joined ThoughtWorks as Chief Scientist in 2000.
evidence_summary: Wikipedia and his own bio confirm birth 18 Dec 1963 and that books and agile prominence arrived in his 30s. Early employment after university is not a material milestone under the strict age-26 rule.

name: Ruth Porat
milestone_by_age_26: Born 1957; married 1983 (age ~26) and began Morgan Stanley career in 1987 (age ~30). Stanford BA, LSE MSc, Wharton MBA preceded banking; major milestones (MS CFO 2010; Google/Alphabet CFO 2015; president/CIO 2023) all well after 26. No material professional milestone by age 26 found.
early_history_summary: Ruth Porat was born in Sale, England to Jewish parents; the family moved to Cambridge, MA then Palo Alto, where her physicist father worked at SLAC. She studied economics/IR at Stanford, industrial relations at LSE, and MBA at Wharton, then built a multi-decade finance career culminating as Google/Alphabet CFO and later president and chief investment officer.
family_context_summary: Born in Sale, Cheshire, England to Dan and Frieda Porat; Jewish family with Holocaust-era refugee father who later worked as a physicist at Harvard then SLAC for 26 years. Brother Marc Porat founded General Magic.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Dan Porat was a research physicist (ion implantation, spark chamber spectrometer work linked to SLAC particle physics); mother born in Mandatory Palestine. Domain is physics/engineering research, adjacent to tech but not finance.
evidence_summary: Wikipedia and NYT wedding notice fix birth ~1957 and 1983 marriage. Career breakthroughs were Wall Street leadership in the 2000s–2010s and Google from 2015—far past age 26.

name: Alexander Rush
milestone_by_age_26: No birth year documented; Harvard BA 2007, MIT PhD 2009–2014, Facebook AI postdoc 2015, Harvard faculty 2015–2019, Cornell associate professor from 2019. Major faculty and open-source impact (Hugging Face) post-PhD—cannot verify a material milestone by age 26 without birth year.
early_history_summary: Alexander (Sasha) M. Rush earned a BA in Computer Science from Harvard (2007) and a PhD from MIT (2014) under Michael Collins on relaxation methods for NLP decoding. After a Facebook AI Research postdoc with Yann LeCun, he was assistant professor at Harvard then associate professor at Cornell Tech, with part-time work at Hugging Face.
evidence_summary: CV and homepage give education/career dates but no birth year. Even if BA at ~22, PhD completion in 2014 and faculty start in 2015 are typically late 20s/30s; no dated ≤26 breakthrough established.

name: Shawn Bohner
milestone_by_age_26: No reliable birth year or dated early career milestone found in reviewed sources. Academic software-engineering profile (Rose-Hulman / Virginia Tech associations) lacks a verified material achievement by age 26.
early_history_summary: Shawn Bohner appears as a professor of computer science and software engineering (e.g., Rose-Hulman Institute of Technology) with publications in software engineering. Public sources provide little biographical detail on early career dates.
evidence_summary: Scholar/ResearchGate profiles and sparse LinkedIn-style hits do not establish birth year or a specific, dual-sourced ≤26 milestone. Marked ineligible under the strict rule.

name: Karen Spärck Jones
milestone_by_age_26: Born 1935; Cambridge history/philosophy 1953–56 (age ~18–21), married Roger Needham 1958 (age 23), CLRU work from late 1950s. PhD-level work Synonymy and Semantic Classification associated with 1964 (age ~28–29); foundational IDF paper 1972 (age 36–37). No material field-defining milestone by age 26 found.
early_history_summary: Karen Ida Boalth Spärck Jones was born in Huddersfield; father was a chemistry lecturer, mother a Norwegian WWII exile. After Girton College Cambridge she briefly taught school, then joined the Cambridge Language Research Unit under Margaret Masterman, building a career in IR and NLP at Cambridge until retirement in 2002.
family_context_summary: Born in Huddersfield, Yorkshire; father Alfred Owen Jones was a chemistry lecturer; mother Ida Spärck fled Norway after the 1940 German invasion and served the Norwegian government in exile in London.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a chemistry lecturer (science teaching, not computing). Mother's wartime public-service experience shaped family resilience but not a computing domain apprenticeship.
evidence_summary: Wikipedia, Cambridge obituary, and NYT Overlooked confirm birth 26 Aug 1935 and that her famous IDF contribution (1972) and published thesis (1964) came after age 26. Early CLRU employment is not itself a material public milestone under the rubric.

name: Tom Gilb
category: Systems engineer / software metrics and evolutionary development
milestone_by_age_26: Born 1940; joined IBM in Norway in 1958 (~age 18) and became a freelance consultant in 1960 (~age 20). Work he is known for—evolutionary development processes from 1968, Software Metrics (1977), Software Inspection (1993)—began at age ~28+. Early employment/consulting alone is not a material field-defining milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Thomas Steven Gilb was born in Pasadena, emigrated to the UK in 1956 and Norway in 1958, joined IBM, then freelanced from 1960. He pioneered evolutionary software delivery (Evo), software metrics, inspection methods, and Planguage, consulting to multinationals and becoming a BCS Honorary Fellow (2012).
evidence_summary: Wikipedia and his site confirm birth 1940 and IBM/freelance dates, but the evolutionary-development and metrics contributions that define his reputation start ~1968 (age 28) and later books. Conservative judgment: age_26_ineligible.

name: Gordon Bell
milestone_by_age_26: Joined Digital Equipment Corporation in summer 1960 at age 25 and designed the I/O subsystem of the PDP-1 (including the first UART), becoming a core early engineer of DEC's pioneering minicomputer line.
early_history_summary: Chester Gordon Bell grew up in Kirksville, Missouri, helping in the family electrical business repairing appliances and wiring homes. He earned BS (1956) and MS (1957) in electrical engineering from MIT, spent a Fulbright year teaching computer design in Australia (1957–58), then worked in MIT's Speech Computation Laboratory before DEC founders Ken Olsen and Harlan Anderson recruited him in 1960.
primary_leverage_engine: Scarce computer architecture skill + early DEC immersion
family_context_summary: Raised in Kirksville, Missouri in a family electrical business (Bell Electric); early hands-on electrical work including professional electrician activity as a youth.
parent_family_domain_summary: Family electrical business provided practical electrical engineering exposure and repair/wiring experience; not a computing company but close domain proximity for digital design.
primary_early_advantage_tags: MIT EE, Fulbright, family electrical business, DEC recruitment, minicomputer wave, hands-on wiring
evidence_summary: Bell combined elite MIT EE training and early computer exposure (Australia Fulbright programming UTECOM/DEUCE; MIT speech lab) with family electrical-shop practice. Recruited into DEC in summer 1960 at age 25, he designed PDP-1 I/O including the first UART and later architected PDP-4 and PDP-6 before returning as VP of Engineering for VAX. He rode the structural minicomputer wave at the frontier firm creating that class. Family provided domain-adjacent electrical skill but not capital or computing networks. Later National Medal of Technology, Computer History Museum founding, and Microsoft Research MyLifeBits work cemented tier-2 status as 'father of the minicomputer.'
starting_point: Born in Kirksville, Missouri into a family electrical business; early hands-on appliance repair and home wiring before MIT electrical engineering.
current_position: Died May 17, 2024 at age 89 in Coronado, California; final roles included researcher emeritus at Microsoft Research and co-founder/board figure of the Computer History Museum.

trajectory.event: Earned BS in electrical engineering from MIT; MS followed in 1957.
Fulbright year in Australia teaching computer design and programming UTECOM (English Electric DEUCE).
Joined DEC in summer 1960; designed PDP-1 I/O subsystem including the first UART.
Left DEC for Carnegie Mellon University to teach computer science after architecting PDP-4 and PDP-6.
Returned to DEC as VP of Engineering, overseeing development of the successful VAX computer systems.
Resigned from DEC after a heart attack; founded Encore Computer (early shared-memory multiprocessors).
Received the U.S. National Medal of Technology for minicomputer architecture contributions.
Died of aspiration pneumonia at home in Coronado, California.

name: Albert F. Case Jr.
milestone_by_age_26: Born March 2, 1955; began software career in 1972 (~age 17) and joined Nastec (CASE tools) in 1982 (~age 26–27). Book Information Systems Development (1986, age ~31) and Gartner leadership came later. No clearly dual-sourced material breakthrough dated at age ≤26 found.
early_history_summary: Albert F. Case Jr. graduated from SUNY Buffalo, started in software in 1972, held roles including MIS director at Ryder and co-founded Maximus Systems. In 1982 he joined Nastec Corporation, a CASE pioneer (DesignAid, LifeCycle Manager), later becoming a long-time Gartner analyst/executive and serial entrepreneur.
evidence_summary: Wikipedia establishes birth 1955 and Nastec join in 1982 (borderline age 26/27 depending on month). His defining CASE advocacy and Prentice Hall book are mid-career. Conservative: age_26_ineligible.

name: Bob Bemer
milestone_by_age_26: Born 1920; BA mathematics Albion College 1940 (age 20) and aeronautical certificate 1941; career as aerodynamicist at Douglas from 1941. Computer-era milestones (RAND 1951 age 31; IBM 1957 age 37; ASCII committee ~1960 age ~40; COBOL contributions) all well after 26. No material computing milestone by age 26 found.
early_history_summary: Robert William Bemer was born in Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan, graduated Cranbrook Kingswood (1936) and Albion College (BA math 1940), then studied aeronautical engineering. He worked as an aerodynamicist at Douglas Aircraft before moving into computing via RAND, IBM, UNIVAC, Bull, GE, and Honeywell, contributing to ASCII, COBOL, and early Y2K awareness.
evidence_summary: Wikipedia and contemporary obituaries document birth 8 Feb 1920 and that fame as 'Father of ASCII' and COBOL committee member came in his late 30s–40s. Early aeronautics career is outside the computing domain for which he is known.
